=== CALL C0507 ===
Agnieszka: Hello! Hi, can you hear me? Sorry, I never know if I do this right, the button for the camera.
Tariq: Yes, I can hear you fine. Hello. I'm Tariq.
Agnieszka: Tariq, lovely. I'm Agnieszka. Erm, is difficult name, everybody here says Aga, is fine, you can say Aga.
Tariq: Agnieszka. I'll try the full one, if that's okay.
Agnieszka: Oh! Very good, very good, nobody does that. So how are you, you are okay? You did the puzzle thing before?
Tariq: I did, yes. I'm well, thank you. The puzzle was, er, harder than I expected towards the end. I ran out of time on the last two.
Agnieszka: Me too! I was like, oh my God, the clock, the clock. I get nervous with the tests, you know, I think somebody is watching me. My son he laugh at me, he says Mum, it's not exam.
Tariq: How old is your son?
Agnieszka: Kacper, he is seventeen, he does plumbing at college. Is good, plumber always has work, I tell him. And my daughter Natalia, she is twenty-one, she moved out last year to Eastleigh with boyfriend. So now is quiet in house, only my husband and Kacper and me. You have children?
Tariq: Two. A son, seventeen as well, doing A-levels. And a daughter, fourteen.
Agnieszka: Seventeen, same! Is hard age, no? They don't tidy, they don't talk, only phone.
Tariq: Mine talks, but mostly to tell me revision is going fine. Which I, er, I have my doubts about.
Agnieszka: Yes, yes, I know this! And what you do, for work? I thought from the picture, maybe teacher, or doctor.
Tariq: No, nothing so noble. I'm a team leader at a contact centre in Stratford. Broadband and mobile. I look after eleven advisers, and I take the difficult calls when a customer wants someone more senior.
Agnieszka: Oh, the angry people. I am sorry for you. I call once for my internet and I was forty minutes waiting with music.
Tariq: That wasn't us, I hope. What do you do?
Agnieszka: I'm cleaner, part-time. Offices and one GP surgery in city centre, in Southampton. I start at six in the morning, sometimes evenings also. Is okay, I like it, I like the reception girls, we talk. But in winter the early bus, oh, is freezing and always late, and is not good for my hands.
Tariq: Six is early. I'd struggle with that.
Agnieszka: You get used. Well, sort of. I would like maybe a school job, daytime, normal hours, you know. That is my dream, not big dream.
Tariq: It sounds like a sensible one, to be honest. Predictable hours matter more than people think.
Agnieszka: Yes! Exactly. And you, you live in London?
Tariq: Ilford. East London. I've been in London about twenty-five years now. I came from Karachi originally.
Agnieszka: Twenty-five! I am almost twenty, from Poland, near Rzeszów. You still feel, erm, like you are from there? Because me, sometimes I don't know. In Poland they say I'm English now, and here I'm Polish.
Tariq: That's, er... yes. I think that's quite precise, actually. When I'm abroad I say I'm a Londoner. When I'm in London I'm Pakistani. It sort of depends who's asking, right?
Agnieszka: Yes, who is asking! I like this. I will say this to my husband.
Tariq: Do you go back often?
Agnieszka: Every summer, two, three weeks. My mum is there, my sister. Mum is alone now since my dad died, so I call her every day, video, long calls. She shows me her garden. You go to Pakistan?
Tariq: Every couple of years. For family. It's more duty than holiday, if I'm honest. When I want a holiday I'd rather go somewhere new. Granada, Istanbul. I spent a whole afternoon at the Alhambra just looking at ceilings.
Agnieszka: Ceilings! Oh, you are the art person. Me, no, I am honest, museums I don't understand. I like my Polish series and the singing in church.
Tariq: That's perfectly fair. Nobody needs to like ceilings.
Agnieszka: My husband likes the ceiling only when it's not leaking! Oh, is it finishing? The timer?
Tariq: I think so. It was nice to meet you, Agnieszka.
Agnieszka: You too, you said my name very good! Bye, bye!

=== CALL C0508 ===
Liam: Hiya, you alright? I'm Liam.
Riya: Hi! Riya. Yeah, good thanks, you?
Liam: Yeah, not bad, not bad. Just recovering from that puzzle, to be fair. The last one with the shapes nearly finished me off.
Riya: Oh my god, same, I literally just guessed the last few. I was like, it's fine, no one's gonna see this.
Liam: No one's gonna see it. There's probably a league table somewhere, knowing my luck. Where are you based then?
Riya: Leyton, East London. You?
Liam: Wakefield, West Yorkshire. So a bit of a way. What do you do, are you working, studying, or...?
Riya: Bit of both, kind of. Final year at Queen Mary, business management, and I work part-time on reception at a dental practice in Stratford.
Liam: No way. A dental practice? My girlfriend Jess is a dental nurse.
Riya: Shut up, really? Okay, so she'll know. The dentists always run late, right? Mine's like twenty minutes behind by ten in the morning, every day. And I'm the one at the front getting the looks.
Liam: Yeah, no, she says exactly that. She reckons reception get it worst, to be fair, cos you're the first face they see.
Riya: Honestly, yeah. Half the job's just calming people down, like, it's fine, it's a check-up, you'll survive. I actually like that bit. The admin, less so. Recall letters, don't ask.
Liam: I won't ask. What are you after when you finish then?
Riya: Erm, good question. Something in marketing, maybe brand partnerships, like beauty or fashion. I'm gonna sort the grad scheme stuff after my dissertation. That's the plan anyway.
Liam: After the dissertation, yeah. Fair. When's that due?
Riya: Don't. April. It's fine. What about you, what do you do?
Liam: So I'm in technical sales, commercial heating and air con. I look after about sixty trade accounts across West Yorkshire, so I'm out on site visits two, three days a week, quoting jobs, that kind of thing. It's a bit of a grind, but I'm top of the board at the minute, so I can't complain. And the car's a perk, I've got the Audi, which Jess thinks is a bit much.
Riya: Ooh, okay, top of the board. Is that like an actual board?
Liam: It's a screen in the office. Which is worse, do you know what I mean? Everyone can see it.
Riya: That's so much pressure, I'd hate that. I'd be bottom, guaranteed.
Liam: Nah, you'd smash it. You're good with people, you can tell. That's ninety percent of sales.
Riya: Aw, thank you. I'll put that on my CV. "Liam from Wakefield says."
Liam: References available on request. So what do you do for fun? London, there must be loads on.
Riya: Erm, honestly, brunch. Way too much brunch. Walthamstow, Hackney. And trashy TV. Are you watching The Traitors?
Liam: Jess has got me on it. I keep saying I'm not into it, and then I'm sat there going, it's him, it's obviously him.
Riya: No, totally, that's how it gets you. Do you go away much? I'm desperate for a proper holiday.
Liam: Yeah, we try and do two a year. Dubai last year, which was unreal, nice hotel, pool on the roof. Marbella the year before.
Riya: Oh my god, Dubai's literally my dream. Like properly, nice hotel, the whole thing. My boyfriend keeps saying we can't afford it.
Liam: That's what Jess says. She wants us saving for a house. She's probably right, to be fair. Don't tell her I said that.
Riya: Your secret's safe. Was that a golf bag behind you, by the way, in your picture?
Liam: It was, yeah. I took it up last year, mostly cos clients play. I'm terrible.
Riya: That's so corporate, I love it.
Liam: Guilty. Oh, is that the timer going?
Riya: I think so, yeah. Nice to meet you!
Liam: You too, Riya. Good luck with the dissertation!

=== CALL C0509 ===
Agnieszka: Hello! Hi! You can hear me okay?
Riya: Hi! Yeah, I can hear you. I'm Riya.
Agnieszka: Riya, lovely name. I'm Agnieszka, but is difficult, you can say Aga. Sorry, my English, is not perfect.
Riya: No, honestly, your English is fine. Agnieszka. Did I say that right?
Agnieszka: Yes! Very good. Two people today say my name properly, I'm so happy. How are you, you are okay?
Riya: Yeah, good thanks! Bit tired, I've got uni stuff, but good. How are you?
Agnieszka: I'm okay, bit knackered, I start work six this morning. I am cleaner, offices and a GP surgery in Southampton. You are student?
Riya: Yeah, final year, business management at Queen Mary. And I work on reception at a dentist's in Stratford, like two days a week.
Agnieszka: Oh, reception! I love the reception girls at my surgery, we always talk in the morning, I know all their birthdays. Is very busy there, always people waiting, always phone ringing.
Riya: Oh my god, yeah, the phone. And my dentist is always like twenty minutes behind, so I'm just sat there smiling at everyone, like, won't be long!
Agnieszka: Won't be long! Yes, they say this also. You know, when I saw your picture, I think, oh, she looks like my daughter Natalia. The hair, the makeup, the eyes like this, with the line.
Riya: Aw, that's so sweet! How old is she?
Agnieszka: Twenty-one. She moved out last year, with boyfriend, to Eastleigh. But she comes every Sunday for dinner, I make rosół, chicken soup, and she takes food home in boxes.
Riya: No way, that's literally me! I go back to my mum's in Harrow most Sundays and I always come home with, like, five tubs of food. And my laundry, if I'm honest.
Agnieszka: The laundry also! Natalia, the same, she brings the bag. What your mum cooks?
Riya: She's Gujarati, so like thepla, which is kind of a flatbread with spices, and undhiyu, which is this veg thing. It's amazing. I can do a basic dal, but it's not the same.
Agnieszka: Is never the same as mum. I make pierogi, big batches, maybe two hundred, and I freeze. Saturday I make with Natalia, she does the folding, I do the dough. Is nice, we talk, you know, like before.
Riya: That's actually so cute. Do you miss her being at home?
Agnieszka: Erm, yes. Sort of. More than I tell her. Now is only my husband and my son, and my son, he don't talk, only phone and PlayStation. You live with your family?
Riya: No, I live with my boyfriend, in Leyton. We moved in like eight months ago, above a dry cleaner's. They start the machines at seven every morning.
Agnieszka: Seven! I am already at work, ha. Your mum, she is happy you live with boyfriend?
Riya: Erm, she's fine. My aunties don't, like, fully know yet. So, you know. It's a whole thing.
Agnieszka: Ah, the aunties. In Poland also, the aunties know everything about everybody. My mum calls me, she tells me who is getting married, who is pregnant, from people I don't remember!
Riya: Oh my god, that's my family group chat. Every day someone's cousin's engaged.
Agnieszka: Exactly! So what you do after university? You have plan?
Riya: Kind of. Something in marketing, maybe for a beauty brand. I'm gonna sort it after my dissertation. That's what I keep saying, anyway.
Agnieszka: You will be fine, you are friendly girl, people like this. Is most important, I think.
Riya: Aw, thank you. You're making me feel better about it, honestly.
Agnieszka: Oh, the timer! Is finishing already?
Riya: I think so. It was so nice talking to you!
Agnieszka: You too, lovely! Good luck with the university, bye bye!

=== CALL C0510 ===
Liam: Hiya, you alright? Liam.
Tariq: Hello, Liam. Tariq. Yes, fine, thank you.
Liam: Nice one. I have to say, mate, I clocked your picture earlier, navy quarter-zip. We've turned up in the same uniform.
Tariq: So I see. I think it's the, er, the official dress code of people who have meetings about targets.
Liam: Ha, yeah, that's exactly it. Is that what you do then, targets?
Tariq: Broadly. I'm a team leader at a contact centre in Stratford. Broadband and mobile, retentions mainly. People call to cancel, and we try to keep them.
Liam: Retentions, right. So you're basically talking people round. That's sales, to be fair.
Tariq: It is, yes, though the company prefers the word "saving". I've got eleven advisers. And I keep my own spreadsheet of their numbers, because I like to know how the month looks before my manager does, you know.
Liam: No, I love that. I'm the same, my CRM is spotless, everyone takes the mick. I'm in technical sales, heating and air con, commercial. About sixty trade accounts round West Yorkshire. Top of the board at the minute, actually.
Tariq: Congratulations. How long can you stay there?
Liam: That's the question, isn't it? It's March, everyone's chasing year end. But I'm going for area sales manager in the next couple of years, so I need to keep it up.
Tariq: Same sort of position for me, operations manager. The trick, I think, is volunteering for the projects that the right people see. Not the ones that are useful. The ones that are visible, right?
Liam: Visible, yeah. That's proper advice, that. I'm writing that down.
Tariq: Don't quote me to anyone senior.
Liam: Ha, I won't. Where are you based, London?
Tariq: Ilford. Twenty-five years, roughly. Originally Karachi. And you?
Liam: Wakefield, born and bred. Do you get up north much?
Tariq: Not often. I've been meaning to go to the Hepworth, actually. Barbara Hepworth, I like her work very much. And the building is supposed to be quite something.
Liam: The Hepworth! I've been, once, when family came over. It was alright. Bit odd, if I'm honest, lots of big holes in rocks. But the building's good, yeah, by the river.
Tariq: Big holes in rocks is, er, not an unfair summary. That's partly the point. You walk round them and the shape changes. It's worth going slowly.
Liam: Fair enough, I'll give it another go. Do you follow football at all?
Tariq: Cricket, mostly. Pakistan first, England second. I'll watch a full Test on catch-up, which my wife considers a medical condition.
Liam: Five days, mate! I can barely do ninety minutes of Leeds, and that's stressful enough. Do you do holidays, or is it all work?
Tariq: I plan them in quite obsessive detail. Rome was the last proper one. A long weekend, but we upgraded the hotel, a terrace looking at the domes. Probably more than we should have spent.
Liam: Nah, that's what it's for though, isn't it? We did Dubai last year, rooftop pool, the lot. I've got a spreadsheet for every trip.
Tariq: A spreadsheet. Then I think we'd get on.
Liam: Ha, definitely. Oh, that's the timer, I think.
Tariq: It is. Good to meet you, Liam. Good luck with the board.
Liam: Cheers, Tariq, you too, mate.

=== CALL C0511 ===
Agnieszka: Hello! Hi, you can hear me? This is my last one, I think I'm getting better with the buttons now.
Liam: Hiya! Yeah, loud and clear. I'm Liam. You alright?
Agnieszka: I'm okay, thank you, bit knackered. I'm Agnieszka, but you can say Aga, is easier.
Liam: Aga, nice one. Where are you calling from, then?
Agnieszka: Southampton. I'm from Poland, but I live here almost twenty years now. You?
Liam: Wakefield, West Yorkshire. And do you know what, I've been to Poland. Krakow, for a mate's stag do. Few years back now.
Agnieszka: Kraków! Look, I have the magnet on my fridge, behind me. Is beautiful city, no? You saw the old town, the castle?
Liam: I saw the old town, yeah. Mostly at night, to be fair. I think there was a castle. I've got a photo of it somewhere, I just don't remember taking it.
Agnieszka: Ha, the stag do, I know, I know. My husband says the English boys in Kraków, every weekend, matching T-shirts.
Liam: Guilty. Ours were bright orange. What do you do for work, Aga?
Agnieszka: I'm cleaner, part-time. Offices and GP surgery in city centre. I start six in the morning, the bus is freezing, but is okay. When I saw your picture I think, oh, he looks like the managers in the office I clean. Very tidy, very nice shoes.
Liam: Ha, I'll take that. Technical sales, heating and air con, so I'm in and out of offices all the time. Out on site visits two or three days a week, I've got the company car, the Audi, so I basically live on the M62.
Agnieszka: My husband also lives in the car! He is delivery driver, the van. He works too many hours, I tell him, Marek, you are not twenty-five any more. He doesn't listen.
Liam: They never listen. My girlfriend Jess says the same to me, mind, I'm at the gym at six before work.
Agnieszka: Six at the gym! For fun? Oh my God. I do only the exercises from the physio, for my hands, and walking on the Common, when my joints are okay. I have arthritis, so some days, erm, is not so good.
Liam: Oh, sorry to hear that. That must be hard with a physical job and all.
Agnieszka: Yes, sometimes. I worry I lose hours, you know. But the supervisor is good. I would like a school job maybe, daytime, not so cold in morning. Anyway! You like football? I think from your picture, the mug, the cup.
Liam: Leeds United mug, yeah, well spotted. Leeds fan for my sins. Do you watch football?
Agnieszka: No, Marek watches. I like the ski jumping, and volleyball, when Poland plays. I am very loud, my son, Kacper, he goes upstairs, he says Mum, the neighbours.
Liam: Ski jumping! I've never actually sat and watched it properly. Is it tense?
Agnieszka: Oh, very! Is like flying, and you think, he will fall, he will fall, and then no, he lands, and I'm screaming in kitchen. Sunday is ski jumping and the rosół, chicken soup, the whole family.
Liam: That sounds like a good Sunday, to be fair. Mine's meal prep. Chicken, rice, veg, in the boxes for the week.
Agnieszka: Every day chicken and rice? No, no, this is sad food. You need the pierogi.
Liam: Jess would agree with you there. She does most of the cooking, I just do a roast and the barbecue. And a curry for tea on a Friday.
Agnieszka: Tea, you say? For dinner? Here in Southampton they say dinner, but my friend from Liverpool also says tea. I was confused first year, I think she invite me for a cup only!
Liam: Ha, no, tea's your proper meal up north. You'd have turned up and got fed, don't worry. Oh, is that the timer?
Agnieszka: Already? Oh, lovely to meet you, Liam. Tell your Jess, more pierogi!
Liam: I will do. Nice to meet you, Aga, look after yourself!

=== CALL C0512 ===
Riya: Hi! Can you hear me?
Tariq: Yes. Hello. I'm Tariq.
Riya: Riya. Nice to meet you. Is this your last one as well?
Tariq: It is. You're the last of the three for me. How have you found it?
Riya: Yeah, actually fine, everyone's been really nice. Where are you based?
Tariq: Ilford. Gants Hill. And I work in Stratford, so I'm on the Central line most days.
Riya: Oh my god, no way, I work in Stratford too. And I'm in Leyton. So we've probably been squashed on the same train.
Tariq: Very likely. Eight-fifteen, westbound, standing with someone's backpack in my face.
Riya: That is literally every morning. What do you do in Stratford?
Tariq: Contact centre. Broadband and mobile. I'm a team leader, eleven advisers, mostly retentions. And you?
Riya: I'm on reception at a dental practice, two days a week, and I'm doing my final year at Queen Mary, business management.
Tariq: Final year. So the dissertation is, er, presumably going well?
Riya: Ha, okay, so, everyone asks that. It's going. Let's say it's going. It's on, like, consumer behaviour in skincare marketing.
Tariq: That's quite a specific topic. Is that where you want to work, then? Brands?
Riya: Yeah, kind of, marketing or brand partnerships, maybe beauty or fashion. I'm gonna look at grad schemes after I hand in. My parents are like, why aren't you applying now, but, you know.
Tariq: I'm afraid I'm probably on your parents' side there. My son is doing A-levels and I say the same thing every evening. He doesn't like it either.
Riya: No, totally, I get it. My dad's a pharmacist and my mum's an accountant, so I think they kind of assumed I'd do one of those. Business was, like, the compromise.
Tariq: My wife works in a pharmacy, actually. Dispensing. She'd tell you it's a respectable life and a very repetitive one.
Riya: That's exactly what my dad says when he's had a long day! So what do you do outside work, are you into anything?
Tariq: Galleries, mostly. I go on my own, on a weekday off. Tate Modern, the Barbican. There's an exhibition coming at the Barbican I've been, er, sort of counting down to.
Riya: Oh, that's nice. I've been to a couple of the immersive ones, like the light ones where you lie on beanbags. Mostly for the pictures, I'm not gonna lie.
Tariq: Honest, at least. I'll admit I'm not their target audience. I prefer the kind where nobody is lying on anything. And you? Weekends?
Riya: Brunch. Walthamstow, mostly, or Hackney. Too much brunch, honestly. And trashy TV with my boyfriend.
Tariq: Walthamstow. There's a Turkish place there near the market I rate very highly. The lamb is excellent. If you ever get bored of brunch.
Riya: Ooh, okay, send me the name. Well, you can't, but, you know. I'll find it.
Tariq: It's on Hoe Street. You'll find it. I think that's our time.
Riya: Oh, yeah. Nice to meet you, Tariq. Good luck with the Barbican thing.
Tariq: Thank you. And with the dissertation. Apply before you hand in.
Riya: Ha, okay, okay. Bye!

It's a bit of a grind, but I'm top of the board at the minute, so I can't complain. And the car's a perk, I've got the Audi, which Jess thinks is a bit much.
Riya: Ooh, okay, top of the board. Is that like an actual board?
Liam: It's a screen in the office. Which is worse, do you know what I mean? Everyone can see it.
Riya: That's so much pressure, I'd hate that. I'd be bottom, guaranteed.
Liam: Nah, you'd smash it. You're good with people, you can tell. That's ninety percent of sales.
Riya: Aw, thank you. I'll put that on my CV. "Liam from Wakefield says."
Liam: References available on request. So what do you do for fun? London, there must be loads on.
Riya: Erm, honestly, brunch. Way too much brunch. Walthamstow, Hackney. And trashy TV. Are you watching The Traitors?
Liam: Jess has got me on it. I keep saying I'm not into it, and then I'm sat there going, it's him, it's obviously him.
Riya: No, totally, that's how it gets you. Do you go away much? I'm desperate for a proper holiday.
Liam: Yeah, we try and do two a year. Dubai last year, which was unreal, nice hotel, pool on the roof. Marbella the year before.
Riya: Oh my god, Dubai's literally my dream. Like properly, nice hotel, the whole thing. My boyfriend keeps saying we can't afford it.
Liam: That's what Jess says. She wants us saving for a house. She's probably right, to be fair. Don't tell her I said that.
Riya: Your secret's safe. Was that a golf bag behind you, by the way, in your picture?
Liam: It was, yeah. I took it up last year, mostly cos clients play. I'm terrible.
Riya: That's so corporate, I love it.
Liam: Guilty. Oh, is that the timer going?
Riya: I think so, yeah. Nice to meet you!
Liam: You too, Riya. Good luck with the dissertation!
calls.C0509:
Agnieszka: Hello! Hi! You can hear me okay?
Riya: Hi! Yeah, I can hear you. I'm Riya.
Agnieszka: Riya, lovely name. I'm Agnieszka, but is difficult, you can say Aga. Sorry, my English, is not perfect.
Riya: No, honestly, your English is fine. Agnieszka. Did I say that right?
Agnieszka: Yes! Very good. Two people today say my name properly, I'm so happy. How are you, you are okay?
Riya: Yeah, good thanks! Bit tired, I've got uni stuff, but good. How are you?
Agnieszka: I'm okay, bit knackered, I start work six this morning. I am cleaner, offices and a GP surgery in Southampton. You are student?
Riya: Yeah, final year, business management at Queen Mary. And I work on reception at a dentist's in Stratford, like two days a week.
Agnieszka: Oh, reception! I love the reception girls at my surgery, we always talk in the morning, I know all their birthdays. Is very busy there, always people waiting, always phone ringing.
Riya: Oh my god, yeah, the phone. And my dentist is always like twenty minutes behind, so I'm just sat there smiling at everyone, like, won't be long!
Agnieszka: Won't be long! Yes, they say this also. You know, when I saw your picture, I think, oh, she looks like my daughter Natalia. The hair, the makeup, the eyes like this, with the line.
Riya: Aw, that's so sweet! How old is she?
Agnieszka: Twenty-one. She moved out last year, with boyfriend, to Eastleigh. But she comes every Sunday for dinner, I make rosół, chicken soup, and she takes food home in boxes.
Riya: No way, that's literally me! I go back to my mum's in Harrow most Sundays and I always come home with, like, five tubs of food. And my laundry, if I'm honest.
Agnieszka: The laundry also! Natalia, the same, she brings the bag. What your mum cooks?
Riya: She's Gujarati, so like thepla, which is kind of a flatbread with spices, and undhiyu, which is this veg thing. It's amazing. I can do a basic dal, but it's not the same.
Agnieszka: Is never the same as mum. I make pierogi, big batches, maybe two hundred, and I freeze. Saturday I make with Natalia, she does the folding, I do the dough. Is nice, we talk, you know, like before.
Riya: That's actually so cute. Do you miss her being at home?
Agnieszka: Erm, yes. Sort of. More than I tell her. Now is only my husband and my son, and my son, he don't talk, only phone and PlayStation. You live with your family?
Riya: No, I live with my boyfriend, in Leyton. We moved in like eight months ago, above a dry cleaner's. They start the machines at seven every morning.
Agnieszka: Seven! I am already at work, ha. Your mum, she is happy you live with boyfriend?
Riya: Erm, she's fine. My aunties don't, like, fully know yet. So, you know. It's a whole thing.
Agnieszka: Ah, the aunties. In Poland also, the aunties know everything about everybody. My mum calls me, she tells me who is getting married, who is pregnant, from people I don't remember!
Riya: Oh my god, that's my family group chat. Every day someone's cousin's engaged.
Agnieszka: Exactly! So what you do after university? You have plan?
Riya: Kind of. Something in marketing, maybe for a beauty brand. I'm gonna sort it after my dissertation. That's what I keep saying, anyway.
Agnieszka: You will be fine, you are friendly girl, people like this. Is most important, I think.
Riya: Aw, thank you. You're making me feel better about it, honestly.
Agnieszka: Oh, the timer! Is finishing already?
Riya: I think so. It was so nice talking to you!
Agnieszka: You too, lovely! Good luck with the university, bye bye!
calls.C0510:
Liam: Hiya, you alright? Liam.
Tariq: Hello, Liam. Tariq. Yes, fine, thank you.
Liam: Nice one. I have to say, mate, I clocked your picture earlier, navy quarter-zip. We've turned up in the same uniform.
Tariq: So I see. I think it's the, er, the official dress code of people who have meetings about targets.
Liam: Ha, yeah, that's exactly it. Is that what you do then, targets?
Tariq: Broadly. I'm a team leader at a contact centre in Stratford. Broadband and mobile, retentions mainly. People call to cancel, and we try to keep them.
Liam: Retentions, right. So you're basically talking people round. That's sales, to be fair.
Tariq: It is, yes, though the company prefers the word "saving". I've got eleven advisers. And I keep my own spreadsheet of their numbers, because I like to know how the month looks before my manager does, you know.
Liam: No, I love that. I'm the same, my CRM is spotless, everyone takes the mick. I'm in technical sales, heating and air con, commercial. About sixty trade accounts round West Yorkshire. Top of the board at the minute, actually.
Tariq: Congratulations. How long can you stay there?
Liam: That's the question, isn't it? It's March, everyone's chasing year end. But I'm going for area sales manager in the next couple of years, so I need to keep it up.
Tariq: Same sort of position for me, operations manager. The trick, I think, is volunteering for the projects that the right people see. Not the ones that are useful. The ones that are visible, right?
Liam: Visible, yeah. That's proper advice, that. I'm writing that down.
Tariq: Don't quote me to anyone senior.
Liam: Ha, I won't. Where are you based, London?
Tariq: Ilford. Twenty-five years, roughly. Originally Karachi. And you?
Liam: Wakefield, born and bred. Do you get up north much?
Tariq: Not often. I've been meaning to go to the Hepworth, actually. Barbara Hepworth, I like her work very much. And the building is supposed to be quite something.
Liam: The Hepworth! I've been, once, when family came over. It was alright. Bit odd, if I'm honest, lots of big holes in rocks. But the building's good, yeah, by the river.
Tariq: Big holes in rocks is, er, not an unfair summary. That's partly the point. You walk round them and the shape changes. It's worth going slowly.
Liam: Fair enough, I'll give it another go. Do you follow football at all?
Tariq: Cricket, mostly. Pakistan first, England second. I'll watch a full Test on catch-up, which my wife considers a medical condition.
Liam: Five days, mate! I can barely do ninety minutes of Leeds, and that's stressful enough. Do you do holidays, or is it all work?
Tariq: I plan them in quite obsessive detail. Rome was the last proper one. A long weekend, but we upgraded the hotel, a terrace looking at the domes. Probably more than we should have spent.
Liam: Nah, that's what it's for though, isn't it? We did Dubai last year, rooftop pool, the lot. I've got a spreadsheet for every trip.
Tariq: A spreadsheet. Then I think we'd get on.
Liam: Ha, definitely. Oh, that's the timer, I think.
Tariq: It is. Good to meet you, Liam. Good luck with the board.
Liam: Cheers, Tariq, you too, mate.
calls.C0511:
Agnieszka: Hello! Hi, you can hear me? This is my last one, I think I'm getting better with the buttons now.
Liam: Hiya! Yeah, loud and clear. I'm Liam. You alright?
Agnieszka: I'm okay, thank you, bit knackered. I'm Agnieszka, but you can say Aga, is easier.
Liam: Aga, nice one. Where are you calling from, then?
Agnieszka: Southampton. I'm from Poland, but I live here almost twenty years now. You?
Liam: Wakefield, West Yorkshire. And do you know what, I've been to Poland. Krakow, for a mate's stag do. Few years back now.
Agnieszka: Kraków! Look, I have the magnet on my fridge, behind me. Is beautiful city, no? You saw the old town, the castle?
Liam: I saw the old town, yeah. Mostly at night, to be fair. I think there was a castle. I've got a photo of it somewhere, I just don't remember taking it.
Agnieszka: Ha, the stag do, I know, I know. My husband says the English boys in Kraków, every weekend, matching T-shirts.
Liam: Guilty. Ours were bright orange. What do you do for work, Aga?
Agnieszka: I'm cleaner, part-time. Offices and GP surgery in city centre. I start six in the morning, the bus is freezing, but is okay. When I saw your picture I think, oh, he looks like the managers in the office I clean. Very tidy, very nice shoes.
Liam: Ha, I'll take that. Technical sales, heating and air con, so I'm in and out of offices all the time. Out on site visits two or three days a week, I've got the company car, the Audi, so I basically live on the M62.
Agnieszka: My husband also lives in the car! He is delivery driver, the van. He works too many hours, I tell him, Marek, you are not twenty-five any more. He doesn't listen.
Liam: They never listen. My girlfriend Jess says the same to me, mind, I'm at the gym at six before work.
Agnieszka: Six at the gym! For fun? Oh my God. I do only the exercises from the physio, for my hands, and walking on the Common, when my joints are okay. I have arthritis, so some days, erm, is not so good.
Liam: Oh, sorry to hear that. That must be hard with a physical job and all.
Agnieszka: Yes, sometimes. I worry I lose hours, you know. But the supervisor is good. I would like a school job maybe, daytime, not so cold in morning. Anyway! You like football? I think from your picture, the mug, the cup.
Liam: Leeds United mug, yeah, well spotted. Leeds fan for my sins. Do you watch football?
Agnieszka: No, Marek watches. I like the ski jumping, and volleyball, when Poland plays. I am very loud, my son, Kacper, he goes upstairs, he says Mum, the neighbours.
Liam: Ski jumping! I've never actually sat and watched it properly. Is it tense?
Agnieszka: Oh, very! Is like flying, and you think, he will fall, he will fall, and then no, he lands, and I'm screaming in kitchen. Sunday is ski jumping and the rosół, chicken soup, the whole family.
Liam: That sounds like a good Sunday, to be fair. Mine's meal prep. Chicken, rice, veg, in the boxes for the week.
Agnieszka: Every day chicken and rice? No, no, this is sad food. You need the pierogi.
Liam: Jess would agree with you there. She does most of the cooking, I just do a roast and the barbecue. And a curry for tea on a Friday.
Agnieszka: Tea, you say? For dinner? Here in Southampton they say dinner, but my friend from Liverpool also says tea. I was confused first year, I think she invite me for a cup only!
Liam: Ha, no, tea's your proper meal up north. You'd have turned up and got fed, don't worry. Oh, is that the timer?
Agnieszka: Already? Oh, lovely to meet you, Liam. Tell your Jess, more pierogi!
Liam: I will do. Nice to meet you, Aga, look after yourself!
calls.C0512:
Riya: Hi! Can you hear me?
Tariq: Yes. Hello. I'm Tariq.
Riya: Riya. Nice to meet you. Is this your last one as well?
Tariq: It is. You're the last of the three for me. How have you found it?
Riya: Yeah, actually fine, everyone's been really nice. Where are you based?
Tariq: Ilford. Gants Hill. And I work in Stratford, so I'm on the Central line most days.
Riya: Oh my god, no way, I work in Stratford too. And I'm in Leyton. So we've probably been squashed on the same train.
Tariq: Very likely. Eight-fifteen, westbound, standing with someone's backpack in my face.
Riya: That is literally every morning. What do you do in Stratford?
Tariq: Contact centre. Broadband and mobile. I'm a team leader, eleven advisers, mostly retentions. And you?
Riya: I'm on reception at a dental practice, two days a week, and I'm doing my final year at Queen Mary, business management.
Tariq: Final year. So the dissertation is, er, presumably going well?
Riya: Ha, okay, so, everyone asks that. It's going. Let's say it's going. It's on, like, consumer behaviour in skincare marketing.
Tariq: That's quite a specific topic. Is that where you want to work, then? Brands?
Riya: Yeah, kind of, marketing or brand partnerships, maybe beauty or fashion. I'm gonna look at grad schemes after I hand in. My parents are like, why aren't you applying now, but, you know.
Tariq: I'm afraid I'm probably on your parents' side there. My son is doing A-levels and I say the same thing every evening. He doesn't like it either.
Riya: No, totally, I get it. My dad's a pharmacist and my mum's an accountant, so I think they kind of assumed I'd do one of those. Business was, like, the compromise.
Tariq: My wife works in a pharmacy, actually. Dispensing. She'd tell you it's a respectable life and a very repetitive one.
Riya: That's exactly what my dad says when he's had a long day! So what do you do outside work, are you into anything?
Tariq: Galleries, mostly. I go on my own, on a weekday off. Tate Modern, the Barbican. There's an exhibition coming at the Barbican I've been, er, sort of counting down to.
Riya: Oh, that's nice. I've been to a couple of the immersive ones, like the light ones where you lie on beanbags. Mostly for the pictures, I'm not gonna lie.
Tariq: Honest, at least. I'll admit I'm not their target audience. I prefer the kind where nobody is lying on anything. And you? Weekends?
Riya: Brunch. Walthamstow, mostly, or Hackney. Too much brunch, honestly. And trashy TV with my boyfriend.
Tariq: Walthamstow. There's a Turkish place there near the market I rate very highly. The lamb is excellent. If you ever get bored of brunch.
Riya: Ooh, okay, send me the name. Well, you can't, but, you know. I'll find it.
Tariq: It's on Hoe Street. You'll find it. I think that's our time.
Riya: Oh, yeah. Nice to meet you, Tariq. Good luck with the Barbican thing.
Tariq: Thank you. And with the dissertation. Apply before you hand in.
Riya: Ha, okay, okay. Bye!

C0507.line_text: I'm cleaner, part-time. Offices and one GP surgery in city centre, in Southampton. I start at six in the morning, sometimes evenings also. Is okay, I like it, I like the reception girls, we talk. But in winter the early bus, oh, is freezing and always late, and is not good for my hands.
C0507.what: She brings both hands up into frame and slowly rubs the knuckles of her right hand with her left thumb, flexing the stiff fingers, and her face tightens in a brief wince before the smile comes back.
